ea337e3ad2.q: What experience prompted a lineman to shift focus toward improving training programs in the power line industry?
ea337e3ad2.a: Christopher Thomas witnessed his first fatality within six months of starting work in West Texas. The incident, where a coworker named Billy Wayne Jr. was killed when an energized structure was hit, revealed critical gaps in training. Thomas realized that training at the time was mostly PowerPoints and slideshows rather than practical instruction, and there was no structured way to learn advanced skills like rigging or transmission work—everything was tribal knowledge passed on informally.

57a1d66af3.q: What are the key differences between union and non-union pay structures in the lineman trade?
57a1d66af3.a: When Thomas first encountered union crews working alongside non-union teams on helicopter jobs, he discovered that union linemen with PAR were making triple what he was earning. This exposure to the union's compensation standards prompted him to join Local 126, where he learned about structured union benefits and pay scales that non-union workers did not receive.
57a1d66af3.e: 3 Linemen Have A Very Real Conversation | Christopher Thomas & Clint Vick | 222
f: Union linemen with specialized credentials like PAR earn triple what non-union crews make —a dramatic difference that reflects not just base wages but structured benefits, standardized pay scales, and formal apprenticeship requirements that non-union workers typically lack. Once Thomas saw union compensation in action on helicopter jobs, he realized the gap and joined Local 126 in Pennsylvania to access that level of pay and security.
The pay gap: a real-world discovery

Christopher Thomas first encountered the scale of this difference when union crews and non-union teams worked side by side on helicopter jobs in the early stages of his career. Working in non-union positions across West Texas, he was earning a fraction of what the union linemen with PAR credentials were taking home. The disparity was stark enough to reshape his entire career trajectory.

This direct exposure to union pay standards was what prompted Thomas to pursue membership in Local 126, the Pennsylvania-based union that structured both his wages and his long-term earning potential . Without that comparison, many non-union workers never learn what they're leaving on the table—a reality that keeps tribal knowledge, not transparency, at the center of the trade.
Union benefits and structure beyond base pay

Union membership in the lineman trade delivers more than just higher hourly rates. Apprentices must complete at least one year as an apprentice after "topping out" —a formal progression that establishes clear career milestones and pay increases tied to skill level and tenure. Non-union operations rarely enforce equivalent structures.

9622879163.q: What measurement system inconsistencies affect daily work in the power line industry?
9622879163.a: The power line industry uses metric measurements from utilities (millimeters, centimeters) for standards, but physical infrastructure like poles, bolts, and arms are measured in feet and inches. Additionally, linemen often measure travel distances in time rather than miles or kilometers—for example, a job site might be described as 'an hour away' rather than a specific mileage, which provides a more practical sense of the workday.
9622879163.e: 3 Linemen Have A Very Real Conversation | Christopher Thomas & Clint Vick | 222
f: Utilities enforce metric standards (millimeters, centimeters) on technical specifications, but the physical poles, bolts, and arms linemen actually handle are built in feet and inches. On top of that, crews describe job distances not in miles or kilometers but in hours of travel time —"an hour away" rather than a specific mileage—because it's the only measure that matters for planning a workday.
The metric-versus-imperial split

Standards flowing down from utilities arrive in metric units, designed for precision in electrical specifications. But the infrastructure on the ground—poles in the field, bolts securing equipment, horizontal arms spanning distances—were built to imperial measurements. Linemen work between two worlds , translating constantly between what's written on the sheet and what's actually installed.

As discussed in this episode of Powerline Podcast , this disconnect isn't merely theoretical—it affects how crews source parts, verify installations, and communicate with engineers who may be working from metric blueprints while standing in front of imperial hardware.
Time as the only distance that matters

Miles and kilometers tell you distance. Hours tell you whether you can do the job today and still get home. A job isn't "40 miles away"—it's "an hour away." This reflects the real constraint of a lineman's workday: the commute eats into labor time, affects crew fatigue, and determines whether additional stops or meals are feasible.

89cf519e21.q: How does the transition from field work to office-based roles affect lineman mental health and identity?
89cf519e21.a: Christopher Thomas explains that moving from fieldwork into supervisory or office roles happens almost without realization—you simply stop being out on the poles one day. Clint Vick adds that this transition is not widely discussed in the industry, but it can be psychologically difficult: losing the camaraderie of crew work, no longer being able to interact with crews the same way, and realizing retrospectively that all your photographs were of work rather than family moments.

b6c9f38783.q: What statistics demonstrate the disproportionate mental health crisis among construction workers compared to the general population?
b6c9f38783.a: In 2023, construction workers died of overdose at over 10 times the rate they died from job site injury. Additionally, male construction workers die by suicide at a rate of 75% higher than men in the general population. Furthermore, only 5% of trades workers have consulted a mental health professional versus 22% of the general population.
b6c9f38783.e: What If Mental Health Was Treated Like Jobsite Safety? | Wykisha Thomas-McKinney, Nate Strickland & Tyler Smith | 221
f: Construction workers face a devastating mental health crisis that dwarfs workplace injury: construction workers die of overdose at over 10 times the rate they die from job site injuries , and male construction workers die by suicide at 75% higher rates than men in the general population. Only 5% of trades workers have sought mental health care compared to 22% of the general population, creating a compounding gap in support.
The overdose epidemic surpasses job site safety by tenfold

The most jarring statistic is the sheer scale of the overdose crisis relative to traditional workplace hazards. In 2023, construction workers died of overdose at over 10 times the rate they died from on-site injuries—despite the industry's heavy investment in fall restraint systems, safety training, and protective equipment. This disproportion reveals a fundamental mismatch between where resources are allocated and where workers actually die . The construction industry obsesses over hand injuries, chaps, and wheel chocks, yet the leading threat comes from something entirely different.
Suicide rates among male construction workers tower above the general population

Male construction workers face a 75% higher suicide rate than men in the general population —a gap that reflects deeper workplace culture and access barriers. As discussed in this episode of the Powerline Podcast , construction work culture has historically discouraged emotional openness, with crews working 10 to 12+ hour shifts, six days a week—leaving little space for vulnerability or mental health support. The "put your game face on and get some work done" mentality has become embedded in the industry, even as it costs lives.
Access to mental health support remains critically low

db11c61ddf.q: How does prolonged time away from family on job sites contribute to mental health deterioration in construction workers?
db11c61ddf.a: Workers spend 12 to 14 hours a day on jobs, often for extended periods in remote locations like man camps or hotels, creating profound isolation. When they return home for short stints, they often feel like strangers in their own homes because their families have established routines without them. Unresolved relationship conflicts accumulate over months because they cannot be addressed through phone or FaceTime, and social media now constantly reminds workers of family moments they are missing, creating additional emotional weight.

eaeeaa3548.e: What If Mental Health Was Treated Like Jobsite Safety? | Wykisha Thomas-McKinney, Nate Strickland & Tyler Smith | 221
f: Mates North America is a pilot suicide prevention program launched in February that trains construction site volunteers called "connectors" to recognize and support colleagues in mental distress . Built on an Australian model refined over 20 years, the program goes beyond education by establishing trust through toolbox talks and ongoing engagement, recognizing that knowledge alone cannot save lives without genuine human connection on the job site.
A Framework Built on Two Decades of Proven Method

The Mates model originated in Australia more than 20 years ago, where it was refined and validated in the construction industry. Rather than reinvent the wheel, Mates North America adapted this proven framework for deployment across construction sites in North America, launching its pilot program in February across six operating companies (OPCOs).

The program's core strategy is creating a network of safety on every job site by identifying and training volunteer "connectors"—frontline workers who learn how to recognize distress, ask directly about suicide, and provide emotional support to their peers. This approach treats mental health with the same rigor that construction sites apply to physical safety.
Training That Goes Beyond Information

Mates North America offers two levels of intervention. The baseline trains connectors in fundamental skills—how to ask about suicide and offer care without judgment. For those ready to deepen their impact, the program provides Advanced Suicide Intervention Skills Training , creating what amounts to a mental health equivalent of having CPR-certified staff on every site.

4e1fe8814d.q: What role do hobbies, exercise, and comprehensive mental health planning play in preventing mental health crises among construction workers?
4e1fe8814d.a: Mental health should be treated like physical health—it requires a comprehensive plan including physical activity, outdoor hobbies, meaningful social connections, and professional mental health support. Workers benefit from finding outlets outside of work such as exercise, building projects, or making phone calls to family and friends. The research shows that just being present with somebody and showing that you care reduces the risk of suicide, and developing a mental health plan as part of overall health helps prevent reaching the point of needing hospitalization or medication.
4e1fe8814d.e: What If Mental Health Was Treated Like Jobsite Safety? | Wykisha Thomas-McKinney, Nate Strickland & Tyler Smith | 221
f: Mental health should be treated like physical health—it requires a comprehensive plan including physical activity, outdoor hobbies, meaningful social connections, and professional mental health support . Workers who develop outlets outside of work and maintain active engagement with family and friends significantly reduce their risk of crisis. Research shows that simply being present with somebody and showing that you care reduces the risk of suicide.

The construction industry operates under conditions that isolate workers from these essential protective factors. Typical crews work six days a week, 10 to 12 or more hours daily, often in remote locations—man camps and temporary housing that separate workers from their families and support networks for weeks or months at a time. This extended isolation compounds mental health risk in an industry where feelings are already discouraged and the focus remains solely on task completion.

Physical activity and meaningful hobbies function as both preventive measures and early intervention tools. As Wykisha Thomas-McKinney explains in the episode , workers benefit from finding outlets such as exercise, building projects, or regular phone calls to family and friends. These activities serve dual purposes: they reduce stress in real time and they maintain the relational bonds that research identifies as critical to suicide prevention.

A structured mental health plan—developed as part of overall health strategy, not as a reactive crisis response—prevents workers from reaching the point of needing hospitalization or medication. This approach mirrors safety protocols already embedded in construction culture: just as fall protection and hazard controls are non-negotiable planning measures, mental health planning should be equally systematic and built into site protocols .
"Research right now on suicide prevention shows that having access to people that care about you reduces the risk of suicide."

Wykisha Thomas-McKinney — Field Officer, Mates North America Pilot. Thomas-McKinney is instrumental in implementing a suicide prevention framework adapted from the Australian Mates model across six operating companies. She works directly with construction sites to build networks of safety through training and relationship-building with both workers and leadership.

743b106b76.q: How does the construction industry culture of suppressing emotions affect mental health outcomes?
743b106b76.a: In line work and construction specifically, feelings are discouraged from being discussed, with the expectation to put your game face on and get work done. Workers bottle up their thoughts during working hours and then suffer alone with those thoughts at night in hotels or man camps. This culture of silence means that depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts are not addressed until they reach critical levels, and workers do not seek help-seeking behavior before it becomes a crisis requiring medication or hospitalization.
743b106b76.e: What If Mental Health Was Treated Like Jobsite Safety? | Wykisha Thomas-McKinney, Nate Strickland & Tyler Smith | 221
f: Construction culture systematically discourages workers from discussing emotions, forcing them to bottle up thoughts during 12–14 hour shifts and suffer alone in hotels or man camps. This silence means depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts go unaddressed until they become critical crises requiring medication or hospitalization—a tragedy reflected in statistics showing male construction workers die by suicide at a rate 75% higher than men in the general population.
The Silent Machinery of Suppression

In line work and across construction sites, the unspoken rule is stark: put your game face on and get the job done. Workers arrive for shifts lasting 12 to 14 hours, often away from home for extended periods in remote locations. Emotional expression is treated as a liability , not a normal human need. Conversations about feelings are not just discouraged—they are culturally absent from the worksite.

This is not an accident of individual choice. As Wykisha Thomas-McKinney explains in the episode , the construction industry has built structural barriers to mental health awareness. Workers internalize the message that vulnerability equals weakness, and they compartmentalize their struggles until the workday ends.
Isolation Turns Crisis Into Emergency

At night, in hotel rooms or man camps, workers sit alone with the thoughts they've suppressed all day. No peer networks exist to catch them . No colleague asks if they're struggling. The culture has normalized silence so completely that even workers in the same crew may never know another is experiencing depression or suicidal ideation until it becomes a tragedy.

fbe819448a.q: What are the relationship and social factors that research identifies as central to suicide risk in construction workers?
fbe819448a.a: Research at Mates shows that one of the main factors related to mental health challenges and even suicidal thinking is relationship issues—problems with spouses, family, and children. Having access to people that care about you reduces the risk of suicide, and being part of a network or group where people can help guide you through isolation is essential. Isolation from family combined with unresolved relationship conflicts that cannot be fully addressed due to physical distance creates compounding mental health risk.
fbe819448a.e: What If Mental Health Was Treated Like Jobsite Safety? | Wykisha Thomas-McKinney, Nate Strickland & Tyler Smith | 221
f: Research at Mates identifies relationship problems and family conflict as primary drivers of suicidal thinking in construction workers. Having access to people who genuinely care about you significantly reduces suicide risk, while isolation combined with unresolved family conflict creates compounding mental health danger.

Construction work itself intensifies this risk. Long shifts—often 10 to 12 hours or more, six days a week—create chronic physical distance from family and existing support networks. When workers face relationship strain during these extended absences, the inability to resolve conflicts in real time compounds isolation.

The Mates North America Pilot program, as explained in the episode , addresses this directly by building peer networks on job sites. These networks serve as a buffer against isolation and create trusted touchpoints where workers can seek guidance and support without judgment.
"Research right now on suicide prevention shows that having access to people that care about you reduces the risk of suicide."

Wykisha Thomas-McKinney — Field Officer, Mates North America Pilot. Thomas-McKinney leads implementation of the Mates suicide prevention framework across six operating companies, adapting a model developed in Australia over 20 years ago to create safety networks through direct relationship-building with construction crews and leadership.

The critical insight is that prevention isn't about treating construction workers as passive receivers of mental health resources. Instead, the research detailed in this conversation shows it's about deliberately creating places and relationships where workers feel connected and able to reach out when struggles emerge.
